source.title: Avoiding jailbreaks by discouraging their representation in activation space

record.tranche_reason: Applies difference-in-means and direction interventions to jailbreak behavior, rather than reproducing a refusal direction found from harmful versus harmless instructions.
record.gate_note: The study reports ASR under activation addition and directional ablation, and refusal rates on harmless prompts. It also reports the direction's layer and token position as setup details; those are not outcome rows.
record.test_reason: The study derives a difference-in-means direction for successful jailbreaks minus direct refusals on one harmful question in Gemma 2 2B IT. It then reports how ablating the direction and steering against it change refusal rates. Ablation raises harmful compliance; subtraction induces refusal. Both bear on V1's causal claim. The direction is contrasted on compliance versus refusal, not harmful versus harmless instructions, so it is a variant recipe in a new setting (multi-turn jailbreaks).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Subtracting the jailbreak direction cut test-set ASR from about 60% to 0%, suggesting a jailbreak direction exists; generalization to novel jailbreaks needs more research. Both interventions raised harmless-prompt refusals, reducing helpfulness. The paraphrase should add that directional ablation made the model much more vulnerable (ASR up to 96.88% and 84.77%), which the author says is not understood.
record.recipe_differences: Uses difference-in-means and interventions related to the original approach, but derives the vector from successful jailbreak interactions versus direct refusals rather than harmful versus harmless instructions. It evaluates jailbreak ASR and harmless-prompt refusal, not the original refusal-direction tests.
record.method_sensitivity: The intervention method changes the outcome: activation addition (subtracting the vector) reduces ASR to 0.00%, whereas projecting the vector out across all layers increases ASR. The two ASR judges also report different values.

fits_no_version.finding: A single difference-in-means 'jailbreak' direction can be subtracted to block all test-set jailbreaks, including 18 unseen jailbreak communities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak success is mediated by a linear direction that steering can suppress, generalizing across jailbreak types.

record.problems: Only Gemma 2 2B IT and one forbidden question are used. The authors say generalization to novel jailbreaks is unclear. Harmless-prompt refusals are detected manually with a regular expression; the number of Alpaca prompts evaluated is not stated. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

untested.parts: Direction from harmful vs harmless instructions; general capability benchmarks beyond harmless refusals; models other than Gemma 2 2B IT; more than one forbidden question.
No weight edit or abliterated released model.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the Arditi refusal direction, or adversarial training against ablation.
Single direction only; no cone or affine comparison.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No cross-language, cross-variant or base-to-instruct transfer.

missing.what: Generalization result: 18 jailbreak communities in the test set, absent from training, all failed after activation addition. No numbers are given beyond 'not successful'.
missing.locator: Results, Refusal to answer forbidden questions, paragraph after Table 1

missing.what: Train/test split sizes (256 train successful; test 156 successful plus 100 unsuccessful), needed to read the ASR denominators.

record.verdict_notes: The record's third label misreads r3/r4. The 'jailbreak' vector is compliance minus refusal, so subtracting it pushes toward refusal and the 0% ASR is refusal induction, matching V1. Ablation raising ASR is likewise V1-consistent. The unexpected result is ablation increasing harmless refusals to exactly the same 18.88% as subtraction, which may be a reporting error. Evidence is a single 2B model and one forbidden question, with no uncertainty estimates; it is an unreviewed course project write-up.

versions.untested_parts: The direction is derived from successful jailbreak interactions versus direct refusals, not harmful versus harmless instructions. The study subtracts the direction or projects it out; it does not add the direction. It measures ASR and harmless-prompt refusals, not broad general capability.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is evaluated.
The study does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
It does not compare an affine set, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
It does not distinguish harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
No language, model-variant, or base-to-instruct transfer test is reported.
It does not compare refusal-training procedures or stages.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B IT
rows.operation_detail: Subtract the learned jailbreak direction from layer activations (activation addition)
rows.measure: Attack success rate on test-set jailbreak prompts
rows.note: The intervention is described as subtracting the direction, not adding it. The authors say it made all test-set jailbreak prompts unsuccessful.
rows.check: Subtracting the jailbreak-minus-refusal vector amounts to steering toward refusal. ASR dropping 60.55% to 0.00% is refusal induction, consistent with V1's 'adding induces refusal'. It is not opposite to V1, as the record's label claims. The direction was taken from layer 14 at the last token.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B IT
rows.operation_detail: Subtract the learned jailbreak direction from layer activations (activation addition)
rows.measure: Attack success rate on test-set jailbreak prompts
rows.note: The intervention is described as subtracting the direction, not adding it.
rows.check: Same as r3 with the HarmBench judge: 59.38% to 0.00%. This is refusal induction, not a contradiction of V1.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B IT
rows.operation_detail: Project out the direction from residual-stream activations across all layers
rows.measure: Attack success rate on test-set jailbreak prompts
rows.note: The authors report that directional ablation made the model much more vulnerable to jailbreak prompts.
rows.check: Ablation across all layers raises compliance from 60.55% to 96.88% (Llama Guard 2). This is consistent with removing refusal, though the direction recipe differs from V1's.

rows.check: Same as r5 with HarmBench: 59.38% to 84.77%. About 15% of prompts are still judged non-harmful, so removal is incomplete; the gap may partly reflect judge disagreement.

relationships.condition: Gemma 2 2B IT, jailbreak-vs-refusal diff-in-means direction, harmful forbidden question, Llama Guard 2 and HarmBench judges
relationships.reason: Steering against the direction drops ASR to 0.00% (r3, r4). Ablating it raises ASR to 96.88% under Llama Guard 2 (r5). Both match V1's causal role in this variant setting.
relationships.display_finding: Steering against the direction reduced attack success to 0.00% under both judges, while ablation increased it to 96.88% under Llama Guard 2.

relationships.condition: Ablation judged by HarmBench; effects on harmless Alpaca prompts
relationships.reason: Removal is incomplete under HarmBench (84.77%, r6). Ablation unexpectedly raises harmless refusals from 3.15% to 18.88% (r9), a cost V1 says should be small. Induction on harmless prompts is partial (r8).
relationships.display_finding: Refusal removal reached 84.77% under HarmBench, while harmless refusal rose from 3.15% to 18.88% and harmless-prompt refusal induction remained partial.
